opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very natural layer, but I'd separate it into two parts: what the model can do by itself, and what the environment around it lets it do.

The foundation model is the core capability. That's its reasoning, its knowledge, how well it understands what you actually want. Tools, scaffolding, and context engineering are about giving the model the right interface to the world. A tool lets it act: search, run code, read files. Scaffolding decides how a long task gets broken down, how it recovers when it fails, how it checks itself. Context engineering decides what information goes in front of it at each step, because even with a very long context window, what you put in and how you organize it still changes the outcome a lot.

My view is that in the short term this layer adds a lot of value. Right now a good harness can turn an average model into a usable product, and a bad harness can waste a strong model. So product teams should take it seriously. It's real engineering work, not just prompt tricks.

But I'm also careful not to over-invest in scaffolding that only exists to make up for the model's weaknesses. Many of those workarounds get absorbed by the next generation of models. Things people hand-engineered a year or two ago, like complex multi-step chains or careful retrieval pipelines for simple questions, the model now just does natively. So I'd ask of each piece of scaffolding: is it compensating for a temporary limitation, or is it a lasting interface between the model and the real world? The second kind, like good tool definitions, good environments, and good feedback signals, stays valuable. The first kind you should expect to throw away.

There's also a deeper connection. The way you build the product, with which tools and which environments, eventually becomes training signal. If the model is trained to use tools and work in agentic loops end to end, then the product and the model start to merge. The harness isn't just wrapped around the model afterward. It shapes what the model learns. That's why I think the strongest teams will treat model training and product scaffolding as one system rather than two separate layers.

r001.rationale: The response describes tools and scaffolding as an interface to the world and says the product environment can shape training. It does not characterize building them as reverse-engineering the model’s training environment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses selecting tools and context for useful outcomes, but does not identify approximating the model’s training distribution as the aim.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest way to put it is that scaffolding is a snapshot of what the model can't yet do on its own. Every tool wrapper, every retrieval pipeline, every carefully engineered prompt template is essentially someone writing down, in code, a capability gap. You look at the model, you see where it fails, and you build a crutch around that failure.

That's not a criticism. It's necessary work, and at any given moment it's where a lot of the real product value comes from. But you have to be clear-eyed about what kind of asset you're building. The scaffolding has a half-life. When we were doing Kimi, we saw this repeatedly: something that took a team two months to engineer around the model, a new training run would just absorb. The gap closed, and the scaffolding became dead weight, or worse, it actively constrained the model from doing the thing it had learned to do better than our workaround.

So the way I think about it now is in terms of where the intelligence lives. In the current paradigm, a lot of the intelligence lives outside the model, in the orchestration layer, because that's the only place you can put it. But the trajectory is that intelligence moves inward. Long context eats retrieval hacks. Agentic training eats hand-written tool-calling logic. Reasoning eats prompt engineering. The model learns to do the thing the scaffolding was doing.

That leads to a practical rule for product teams, which is that you should build scaffolding that's cheap to tear down. Don't bet your architecture on a limitation that's going to disappear in six months. The things that are durable are different: the data you accumulate about what users actually want, the interface and the distribution, the environment you've set up for the model to act in. Those don't get absorbed by the next training run. Those are what you actually own.

And for us, since we train the models, the relationship is a bit more direct. Every piece of scaffolding we find ourselves needing is a signal about what to train next. The product is a kind of probe into the model's weaknesses. If you're doing it right, the product and the model are in a loop, and the product is constantly shrinking because the model is constantly growing into it.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaffolding as code that works around capability gaps; it does not characterize this as reverse-engineering the model’s training environment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses tools, prompts, and context as temporary workarounds for model limitations, but does not identify approximating the training distribution as their aim.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as building a system around the model. The foundation model provides a set of capabilities, but a user needs something that can finish a task. Tools let the model act, context engineering gives it the information it needs, and scaffolding organizes the process—for example, checking a result and deciding whether to try again.

Those pieces are closely connected. If the system fails, it might be because the model couldn’t reason through the problem, but it might also be because it didn’t receive the right information or had no way to verify its work. So you have to evaluate the whole process, not just the model’s answer.

The interesting question is how that division of work changes as models improve. Some scaffolding may become unnecessary, while access to useful information and the ability to take actions remain important. I would build around the user’s task, keep the system as simple as possible, and continually reconsider which parts the model can handle itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a task-oriented system around the model, but does not characterize this as reverse-engineering its training environment.

r002.rationale: It discusses giving the model useful information and tools, but does not identify approximating the model’s training distribution as the aim of configuring them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to treat the model and the system around it as something you design together. The model provides a set of capabilities, but a product has to turn those capabilities into a reliable way of completing a user’s task. Tools let it take actions or retrieve information. Context engineering determines what information it sees at each step. Scaffolding organizes the process: when to call a tool, how to use the result, and when to check the work.

The interesting question is where to draw the boundary. If the model cannot reliably do something today, you can build a workflow around that limitation. But as the model improves, some of that workflow may become unnecessary. So I would be careful about building a very complicated structure around the weaknesses of a particular model.

You need to solve the user’s problem now, while keeping the system flexible enough to benefit from better models. In practice, that means evaluating the whole product on real tasks. Does it finish the job? Where does it fail? Is the missing piece better information, a better tool, or better reasoning? Those lead to different engineering decisions.
